title: When I was little: the imperfect
why: After the perfecto and the indefinido, here's the third past tense, the imperfecto, used to describe things and talk about past habits: what English says with “used to”, “would” or “was …ing”. With only three irregular verbs (era, iba, veía), you can talk about your childhood, your school and your vacations at your grandparents', before learning to combine it with the indefinido.

The imperfect: a very regular conjugation

The imperfecto has no single English equivalent: it covers “I used to play”, “I would play (every summer)”, “I was playing” and often a plain “I played” when it means a habit or a description. The good news: it's the easiest tense in Spanish, with two sets of endings, one for -ar and one for -er / -ir.

jugarcomervivir
yojugabacomíavivía
tújugabascomíasvivías
él, ella, ustedjugabacomíavivía
nosotros, nosotrasjugábamoscomíamosvivíamos
vosotros, vosotrasjugabaiscomíaisvivíais
ellos, ellas, ustedesjugabancomíanvivían

What to watch

  • -ar verbs are spelled with a b: jugaba, hablaba, never with a v.
  • Only the nosotros form of -ar verbs has an accent: jugábamos, estábamos.
  • For -er and -ir, every form has an accent on the í: comía, vivíamos, teníais.
  • The yo and él forms are identical (jugaba): add the subject if the sentence isn't clear.

No stem changes in the imperfect: jugar → jugaba, dormir → dormía, querer → quería. And you already know quería: it's the polite “I'd like” you use in cafés and shops.

", "

Only three irregular verbs: era, iba, veía

In the whole language, only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect. Even tener, hacer or estar, so complicated in the indefinido, are perfectly regular here: tenía, hacía, estaba.

serirver
yoeraibaveía
túerasibasveías
él, ella, ustederaibaveía
nosotros, nosotraséramosíbamosveíamos
vosotros, vosotraseraisibaisveíais
ellos, ellas, ustedeseranibanveían
De pequeño era muy tímido, iba al colegio a pie y veía dibujos animados todas las tardes.As a kid, I was very shy, I used to walk to school and I watched cartoons every afternoon.

And hay? In the imperfect, it becomes había: En mi pueblo había un río. (In my village there was a river.) Just one form, even before a plural: había muchos niños (there were lots of kids).

Compare with the indefinido from the previous lessons: fui (I went, once) / iba (I used to go, I was going); tuve (I had, I got, at one point) / tenía (I had, over a period).

", "

When to use it

The imperfect describes the past and talks about things that happened repeatedly. Here's the trap for English speakers: English often uses the plain past for these (“When I was a kid, I played outside”), but Spanish needs the imperfect. The test: if you could say “used to”, “would” or “was …ing”, use the imperfect (“I used to do” → hacía); if you're describing how things were, use it too.

UseExampleTranslation
a past habitDe pequeña jugaba en la calle.As a little girl, I used to play in the street.
a descriptionLa casa era grande y tenía un jardín.The house was big and had a garden.
the weatherHacía calor y el cielo estaba azul.It was hot and the sky was blue.
ageTenía diez años.I was ten years old.
the timeEra la una. Eran las ocho.It was one o'clock. It was eight o'clock.

Habit markers

de pequeño / de pequeña, de niño / de niña (as a child, when I was little), antes (before, in the past), siempre, a menudo (often), todos los veranos, los domingos, cuando era joven.

Note: de pequeño replaces a whole clause, like English “as a child”. No need to say “cuando yo era pequeño”, even though that's correct too.

Soler + infinitive

To say “to usually do” or “used to”, Spanish has a verb: soler. In the imperfect, it's regular: solía, solías, solía, solíamos, solíais, solían.

Los domingos solíamos comer en casa de mis abuelos.On Sundays we used to have lunch at my grandparents' house.

For age, Spanish uses tener: tenía diez años (literally “I had ten years”), never “era diez años”, even though English says “I was ten”. And for the time, era la una but eran las dos, as in the present.
